name: The Old Yew of Cremines (If millenaire)

location.address: Foret du Maljon, above Cremines, Bernese Jura

access: Free, public forest (Foret du Maljon). No path or signposts lead to it directly; the commune's own page says it stands hidden under rocks, off the walking paths, deliberately hard to find. Public land, not private, but expect a real search on foot.
transport: No public transport nearby; nearest station is Cremines on the Moutier-Solothurn line, then on foot up into the Maljon forest (steep, unmarked, roughly 45-60 min walk based on hiking-site descriptions; not verified by us step by step).
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely: the Cremines commune's own page (cremines.ch/if_millenaire.html) calls it 'le plus vieil arbre de Suisse' (the oldest tree in Switzerland), designated 'arbre monumental' by the Bern canton forestry division (Division forestiere du Canton de Berne), estimated age 'environ 1500 ans'. Baumkunde.de's register (entry 2085, last updated 2026-01-26, i.e. reads as recently maintained) independently gives the same coordinates (E7 28.2884' / N47 16.3625', converted here to decimal), age 1500 years, girth 4.25m, condition 'vital' (alive), access 'publicly accessible'. A WebSearch summary of a Solothurner Zeitung feature ('1500 Jahre alt: zu Besuch bei der alten Dame von Cremines, dem aeltesten Baum der Schweiz') corroborates the same figures but the article itself sits behind a Cloudflare challenge and could not be fetched directly, so its specific quotes are not used per the search-summary-is-a-lead rule; only the commune and baumkunde pages are cited as sources. The commune page also lists TV coverage as recent as July 2023 (Canal Alpha), which is the best evidence of continued presence: alive as of at least mid-2023. Exact ring-count dating is impossible because coring the hollow, damage-prone trunk is not done; the 1500-year figure is the commune's and dendrology community's own estimate, not derived by us. Species is common/European yew (Taxus baccata, 'Gemeine Eibe' / 'if'). The tree is genuinely remarkable: candidate for oldest living tree in Switzerland, which clears the single-tree destination bar on its own. Container: no published Swiss city sits within a reasonable day trip (Geneva and Zurich are both 100km+ away); this stands alone.

name: The Marthalen Oak

location.address: Abistwald forest, reached via the FC Ellikon/Marthalen football pitch, Marthalen

access: Free, in a public forest (Abistwald). The local museum's own visitor page says the path there crosses the FC Ellikon/Marthalen football pitch, and jokingly advises bringing a football along; no gate, ticket or restriction is mentioned.
transport: Marthalen railway station (Zurich-Schaffhausen line, roughly 25-30 min from Zurich HB) then on foot into the Abistwald, direction and distance not independently verified by us.
verify_notes: Only one real independent source found despite several searches: the Ortsmuseum Marthalen (the village's own heritage museum)'s 'Entdecken' page, which calls it 'eine der aeltesten Eichen der Schweiz (ueber 360 Jahre)' (one of the oldest oaks in Switzerland, over 360 years), diameter 1.80m. Diameter times pi gives ~5.65m, which matches the circumference figure (~5.60m) repeated across several tourism/regional pages (Zuercher Weinland region, Andelfinger Zeitung mentions), all of which read as downstream copies of the same museum page rather than independent verification, so they are not counted as a second source. The municipality's own forest-inventory page (marthalen.ch) independently confirms the Abistwald holds an unusual number of very large trees ('Stufe 25', diameter over 112cm at breast height, vorwiegend Eichen/predominantly oaks, 44 stems canton-wide category') without naming this specific tree, which supports plausibility but is not itself a second source for this individual tree. Species could not be pinned to a specific oak (Quercus robur vs petraea); left as Quercus sp. per the lead's own genus-only basis, page should ask the reader. Coordinates are from three Commons photographs (panoramio geotags) clustering at this point, which is mapped-photo-level evidence per the aerial/photo evidence standard, so marked confirmed. No dated recent source found to confirm the tree is alive today beyond the museum page itself (undated, but reads as the museum's current visitor guide); flagged for that reason as well as for the single-source evidence. The municipality's own coat of arms depicts an oak, which is suggestive of local significance but not itself evidence about this specific tree. Container: Marthalen sits roughly 30km / about 25-30 minutes by direct train from Zurich (Zurich-Schaffhausen line), which is within the day-trip boundary; recommend it join Zurich's page as a day-trip addition, labeled honestly as Marthalen with its real travel time, the way Blarney and Fota join Cork.
container: zurich (day trip, ~25-30 min by train, label as Marthalen)

name: The Plane Tree of the Ile de Peilz

location.address: Viewed from the Quai Grand Rive shoreline, Villeneuve, looking out to the Ile de Peilz islet in Lake Geneva

access: Free, view-only. Both sources are explicit that the islet itself cannot be visited (2tout2rien.fr: "L'ilot ne se visite pas"; Wikipedia: boat approach risks running aground and is not recommended). It is viewed from the public lakefront quays of Villeneuve (Quai Grand Rive is named as the classic viewpoint) or from a boat on the lake, best at sunrise or sunset when the tree silhouettes.
transport: Villeneuve VD railway station, then a short walk along the lakefront quay.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree: an English Wikipedia article on the islet itself, and a 2026-current French travel-blog piece (2tout2rien.fr) that cites a 2023 certified-arborist health assessment finding the tree 'globalement en bonne sante' (generally healthy) with some decay present but functional, which is the best available 'alive now' evidence and is dated within the last few years. The islet, roughly 20-77 sqm depending on source, is the smallest and only natural island in Lake Geneva; a rock built up with earth by Villeneuve residents (local tradition dates this to 1797, unconfirmed by primary sources). Three plane trees were planted in 1851 (this is a documented planting date for these specific trees, not a park-wide bridge claim); by 1970 only one plane and a sickly horse-chestnut remained, and the chestnut has since died, leaving the single plane tree alone today, hence the ~175-year age used here. Wikipedia gives the island's own coordinates as 46 24'00"N 6 54'50"E (46.4000, 6.9139), about 800m from the Commons-photo-geotagged coordinate used here, which reads as the shore photography spot rather than the island itself; location_precision is 'approximate' because this pins the public viewing shoreline, not a confirmed exact spot, and the exact best vantage (Quai Grand Rive) was named by a search summary rather than fetched directly, so treat the coordinate as indicative only. Species is London Plane per hard rule 9's canonical naming (Wikipedia's 'platane' / 2tout2rien's 'platane'). Genuinely a single-tree destination: referenced in Byron's The Prisoner of Chillon (1816) and Hans Christian Andersen's The Ice-Maiden (1861), and has become a real Instagram photography destination since 2021 per Wikipedia. Not ancient (only ~175 years) but qualifies on visual spectacle, a real superlative (smallest/only natural island in the lake) and documented literary fame rather than age. This is a view-only entry per the 2026-08-13 ruling: the pin marks the viewing place, not the trunk, and access says plainly the island cannot be reached.

name: The Linden of Morat
age_estimate: planted 1984, a direct cutting of a tree first recorded in the 15th century

location.address: Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville, next to the Fontaine Saint-Georges, Bourg quarter, Fribourg

access: Free, a public town square in the historic Bourg quarter of Fribourg.
transport: Fribourg/Freiburg railway station, then roughly a 15-20 minute walk down into the Bourg quarter (not independently timed by us).
verify_notes: This is a living-replanting case, the same pattern CLAUDE.md already blesses for the Elm of Saint-Gervais: the ORIGINAL tilleul de Morat, planted in the Bourg quarter in the 15th century and tied to the legend of a messenger who ran from the 1476 Battle of Morat (Charles the Bold's defeat) to Fribourg waving a linden branch cut from the battlefield, which supposedly took root where he collapsed, was damaged by a vehicle in 1983 and felled. A cutting preserved by the University of Fribourg's Botanical Garden was planted in its place in 1984 'sur la place de l'Hotel-de-Ville... a cote de la fontaine de Saint-Georges, ou il trone encore' (still stands there today) per a directly fetched 2026 watson.ch article marking the battle's 550th anniversary. That is the living tree this entry describes, roughly 42 years old as of 2026, not the medieval original. Only one source was directly fetched and quoted (watson.ch); several other named outlets (La Liberte, La Tele, Batimag) independently cover the same 550th-anniversary story with matching facts per search results, but per the search-summary-is-a-lead rule their specific figures are not used here, only watson's directly-quoted ones, so this is flagged as effectively single-sourced for now. A second, newly planted cutting is being installed in 2026 about 100m away near Rue des Alpes as part of the same anniversary; that is a brand new sapling with no age of its own and is not this entry. Species is only ever called 'tilleul' (lime/linden) in every source found; no source names Tilia cordata vs platyphyllos, so left as Tilia sp. per the lead's own genus-only basis. Location_precision is 'approximate': the square and the named fountain beside it are a precise, findable public landmark, but no source gives GPS coordinates for the tree itself and the coordinate used here comes from Commons photo geotags (files named for the 'Nova-Friburgo-Platz' and the 'Rathaus', which is Fribourg's Hotel-de-Ville in German, consistent with this location) rather than a register or a source-stated position. Genuinely a single-tree destination on historical grounds: a documented civic legend around a real, named battle, an RTS television segment, a museum exhibition ('Une exposition pour celebrer le tilleul de Morat'), and a 550th-anniversary civic replanting ceremony in 2026, which together clear the destination bar even though the living tree itself is not old. Container: Fribourg is roughly 100km from both Geneva and Zurich, the only two published Swiss cities, well outside any day-trip boundary, so this stands alone.

name: The Linden of Linn
access: Free, public. Directly at the 'Boezberg, Linn' bus stop, marking the village entrance; also reachable on a 20-minute waymarked walk from Boezberg-Neustalden station. Aargau Tourismus's own page (updated 2026-08-04) notes it is 'very popular and well-visited', suggesting a weekday or early Sunday visit for a quieter one.
transport: From Zurich: train to Brugg, then onward bus/local transport toward Boezberg/Linn; total journey likely 45-60 minutes each way (not independently timed step by step by us; this is a longer trip than the classic 30-minute day-trip case and should be labelled honestly as such).
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely: German Wikipedia (Linner Linde) gives precise coordinates (47 28'15.1"N 8 7'58.6"O, converted here to decimal), species Sommerlinde/Tilia platyphyllos, height 25m, trunk circumference 11m ('gilt sie als der maechtigste Baum des Aargaus', considered Aargau's mightiest tree), age approximately 800 years, and notes a local legend (plague survivors planting it, 16th/17th century) that the tree's own real age contradicts, which is exactly the kind of legend-vs-dating gap this project should state rather than resolve; the 800-year figure is the tree's own accepted estimate, not derived by us from girth. Aargau Tourismus's official page (aargautourismus.ch, last updated 2026-08-04, i.e. current) independently confirms the ~800-year age, gives the address (Linn 51, 5225 Boezberg) and access details, and its 2026 update date is the best 'alive now' evidence found. A WebSearch summary (not independently fetched, so not used for any figure here) additionally called it 'one of the five oldest trees in Switzerland'; that specific ranking claim is not used per the search-summary-is-a-lead rule, only the two directly fetched sources' own figures are. Girth 1100cm (11m) is unusually large but is stated directly and identically by both fetched sources, and matches the species (Tilia platyphyllos routinely produces very wide, fluted, multi-stemmed trunks at great age), so no unit-corruption flag is warranted; recorded as given. Local legend: the linden's shadow must fall on Habsburg Castle every year or 'the world will end', tying it to Rudolf von Habsburg, founder of the Habsburg dynasty; a good story-worthy fact, stated as legend not history. Container: straight-line distance to Zurich is approximately 32km, just over the usual 30km/30-minute day-trip guideline, and the real journey (train to Brugg plus a further bus/local connection) likely runs 45-60 minutes each way rather than a clean 30; recommend it join Zurich's page as a day-trip addition if the orchestrating session is comfortable with that longer real travel time, labelled honestly as Linn/Boezberg with the true journey time, not as a shorter or in-town trip.
container: zurich (day trip, borderline distance ~32km / real journey likely 45-60 min via Brugg, label honestly as Linn/Boezberg; flagging for a judgement call rather than asserting confidently)
